sandhi.note: Visarga before t becomes s; then ā + u → o (तथा + उरसः → तथोरसः).

samasa.type: caturthī tatpuruṣa (an अर्थ-compound, which grammarians treat as always compounded)
samasa.alt: Also analysed as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, प्रबोधनस्य अर्थः, ‘the purpose of waking’, put in the dative. The sense is the same; the caturthī analysis is the grammarians’ usual one for अर्थ in this use. The same word-form, विबोधनार्थाय, stands in 1.70.

samasa.vigraha: नेत्रे च आस्यं च नासिका च बाहू च हृदयं च, तेभ्यः
samasa.literal: from eyes, mouth, nose, arms and heart
samasa.sense: from every seat of sleep in Viṣṇu’s body; उरस् (chest) follows outside the compound

morph.note: Infinitive of नि + √हन्: the prefix नि- intensifies (‘strike down, slay’). It stands beside a dative of purpose (प्रबोधनार्थाय) with the same function: two purposes, waking and slaying.
Ablative singular of the s-stem उरस् ‘chest’. It is left outside the dvandva, joined by तथा — a common way of completing a list in verse.

mantras.anvaya: (सा देवी) विष्णोः प्रबोधनार्थाय मधुकैटभौ निहन्तुं (च) नेत्रास्यनासिकाबाहुहृदयेभ्यः तथा उरसः (निर्गम्य) —
mantras.anvaya_en: Two expressions of purpose and two ablatives of separation; the absolutive निर्गम्य that governs the ablatives comes at the start of 1.91.
mantras.lit: for the sake of awakening Viṣṇu, to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha, from (his) eyes, mouth, nose, arms and heart, and likewise from (his) chest
mantras.tr: so that Viṣṇu might wake and slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha, came forth from his eyes, mouth, nose, arms and heart, and from his breast,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Came forth’ is supplied from निर्गम्य at the start of 1.91; ‘his’ (Viṣṇu’s) is understood.

comm.t: The Goddess grants both requests of the hymn. She withdraws from Viṣṇu’s body, limb by limb — eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart, chest — so that he wakes, and wakes in order to kill the two asuras.
Brahmā had praised her as dwelling in Hari’s eyes (हरिनेत्रकृतालयाम्, 1.70); the eyes stand first here as she leaves. Sleep is pictured as a presence in the body that departs by every organ.

sandhi.note: -aḥ before a becomes -o and the following a is elided (avagraha).
Final t before the nasal n becomes n. The rule is optional (जगद्नाथ is possible), but the nasal form is usual.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (अव्यक्त itself a nañ tatpuruṣa: न व्यक्तम्)
samasa.literal: of him whose birth is unmanifest
samasa.sense: of Brahmā, whose origin is beyond perception
samasa.alt: Also read as a vyadhikaraṇa bahuvrīhi, अव्यक्तात् जन्म यस्य सः, ‘whose birth is from the Unmanifest (avyakta, primal nature)’. Both readings are found for this epithet of Brahmā; the first keeps the members in the same case and is the simpler analysis.

morph.note: Absolutive with a prefix takes -य (ल्यप्) instead of -त्वा. With √गम् the root nasal may stay (निर्गम्य) or drop (निर्गत्य).

Perfect of √स्था: the reduplicated syllable is त — when a root begins with a sibilant + stop, the stop is repeated, without aspiration (थ् → त्): तस्थौ, with the ending -औ. With उद्, the d becomes t before t (खरि च, 8.4.55): उत्तस्थौ ‘rose’.
Past participle of √मुच्: च् becomes क् before त (मुच् + त → मुक्त). With the instrumental तया: ‘released by her’.

mantras.anvaya: (सा) निर्गम्य अव्यक्तजन्मनः ब्रह्मणः दर्शने तस्थौ। तया मुक्तः जगन्नाथः जनार्दनः च उत्तस्थौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses joined by च, each ending in the perfect of √स्था — तस्थौ (she stood) and उत्तस्थौ (he rose).
mantras.lit: having come out, (she) stood in the sight of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest. And Janārdana, lord of the world, released by her, rose up
mantras.tr: and stood before the eyes of Brahmā, whose birth is beyond knowing. Released by her, Janārdana, lord of the world, rose
mantras.tr_note: ‘Came forth’ was given in 1.90; the verse continues into 1.92 (‘from his serpent couch on the one ocean’).

comm.t: Two movements answer each other: she comes out and stands where Brahmā can see her (तस्थौ), and Viṣṇu, freed, rises (उत्तस्थौ). The Goddess praised in the hymn is now visible to the one who praised her.

Medhas had said that the Goddess, though eternal, is spoken of as ‘born’ whenever she appears for the gods’ work (1.65–66). This is the first such appearance: not a birth, but a coming forth from where she already was.

sandhi.note: -e + a- → -e’-: the initial a is elided (avagraha).
Final t before the unvoiced t stays t; the two words are only written together.
The visarga of सः is dropped before a consonant. ततः before s keeps its visarga (the optional s-assimilation is not used).
Final au before a vowel becomes āv.

samasa.sense: on the single ocean of the dissolution, when the world is all water (एकार्णवीकृते, 1.66)

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (avadhāraṇa: ‘the serpent, which is the couch’)
samasa.sense: from Śeṣa, the serpent on which Viṣṇu sleeps (आस्तीर्य शेषम्, 1.67)
samasa.alt: Also possible as a saptamī tatpuruṣa with शयन as an action noun, अहौ शयनम् ‘lying on the serpent’: ‘from (his) lying on the serpent’. The karmadhāraya fits the ablative of place better.

samasa.vigraha: वीर्यं च पराक्रमः च वीर्यपराक्रमौ; अतिशयितौ वीर्यपराक्रमौ ययोः तौ
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi containing an itaretara dvandva (वीर्यपराक्रम) and the prefix अति
samasa.literal: whose strength and valour are surpassing

morph.note: Perfect of √दृश् with reduplication (द-दृश्-) and the ātmanepada ending -ए. √दृश् is parasmaipada (active perfect ददर्श), and ददृशे normally means ‘was seen’. Here the subject is सः and the object तौ is accusative, so the sense must be active, ‘he saw’ — an epic (ārṣa) use of the middle ending.
Accusative dual of the n-stem आत्मन् at the end of a bahuvrīhi: -आनौ (strong stem).

mantras.anvaya: (सः) एकार्णवे अहिशयनात् (उत्तस्थौ)। ततः सः दुरात्मानौ अतिवीर्यपराक्रमौ तौ मधुकैटभौ च ददृशे —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first two words complete 1.91 (‘rose … from the serpent-couch on the one ocean’). Then a new clause: subject सः, verb ददृशे, and the object तौ with its appositions running into the second line.
mantras.lit: from the serpent-couch on the single ocean. Then he saw those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, evil-minded, of surpassing strength and valour,
mantras.tr: from his serpent couch on the one ocean. Then he saw the two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, evil-hearted and of surpassing strength and prowess,

comm.t: Viṣṇu rises from Śeṣa on the cosmic waters and, for the first time, sees the two asuras who were about to kill Brahmā. The verse sets the scene of the fight: one ocean, no land.
The pāda मधुकैटभौ दुरात्मानौ has nine syllables, one more than the anuṣṭubh pāda; every witness reads it so (see corrections.json, metre notes). The text is kept as it stands.

flags.uncertain: Metre: the pāda मधुकैटभौ दुरात्मानौ is hypermetric (nine syllables) in every witness; no emendation is made. ददृशे is taken as active (‘saw’) with an ātmanepada ending, as the accusative तौ requires.

sandhi.note: Final au before a vowel becomes āv; the m of अत्तुम् becomes anusvāra before b (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).
a + ī → e. Likewise जनित + उद्यम → जनितोद्यम (a + u → o).

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its first part क्रोधरक्त is a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa: क्रोधेन रक्ते)
samasa.literal: whose eyes are red with anger
by whom an effort had been produced
samasa.sense: having set about it, ready to strike

morph.note: Perfect ātmanepada of √युध्, reduplicated यु-युध्-; √युध् is conjugated in the middle (युध्यते). With the instrumental ताभ्याम् it means ‘fought with them’.
सम् + उद् + √स्था with ल्यप्: after उद् the s of स्था drops (उद् + स्था → उत्था), giving उत्थाय ‘having risen’.
Infinitive of √अद्: अद् + तुम् with d unvoiced before t. In 1.68 the two were ready ‘to kill’ Brahmā (हन्तुम्); here they are ready ‘to devour’ him.

mantras.anvaya: (तौ) क्रोधरक्तेक्षणौ ब्रह्माणम् अत्तुं जनितोद्यमौ (ददृशे)। ततः भगवान् हरिः समुत्थाय ताभ्यां युयुधे।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line still describes the object of ददृशे (1.92); the second is a new sentence with an absolutive (समुत्थाय) and the main verb युयुधे.
mantras.lit: with eyes red with anger, having set about devouring Brahmā. Having risen up, then, the Blessed Hari fought with the two
mantras.tr: their eyes red with rage, bent on devouring Brahmā. Rising up, the Lord Hari then fought with them
mantras.tr_note: The fight’s duration and manner follow in 1.94.

comm.t: The danger is at its height: the asuras, eyes red with fury, are about to eat Brahmā. Viṣṇu stands up and fights them himself.
A modern reflection: the hymn’s two requests are now visible as events — the god is awake and acts. The Goddess has not fought; she has made the fight possible.

sandhi.note: au before a becomes āv (तौ + अपि → तावपि); then i before a becomes y (अपि + अति → अप्यति).

samasa.alt: The printed text writes पञ्चवर्षसहस्राणि as one; it could be taken as a single numeral compound (dvigu type). A dvigu proper is a collective singular, so with the plural ending the numeral is more naturally a separate word qualifying वर्षसहस्राणि, as here; the sense is unchanged.

samasa.literal: he whose weapons are his arms

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa, with a prādi tatpuruṣa (अतिबल) as first member
samasa.alt: Also possible: अतिबलौ च उन्मत्तौ च, ‘exceedingly strong and maddened’ (karmadhāraya of two adjectives). The instrumental reading gives the cause of their madness, which the story bears out.

samasa.sense: bewildered by Mahāmāyā, as Brahmā had asked (मोहयैतौ, 1.86)

morph.note: Accusative of extent of time: ‘for (five) thousands of years’.
विमोहित is the past participle of the causative of वि + √मुह् (‘made to be bewildered’); the causative agent stands in the compound’s first member, महामाया.

mantras.anvaya: (सः) विभुः बाहुप्रहरणः पञ्च वर्षसहस्राणि (ताभ्यां युयुधे)। अतिबलोन्मत्तौ महामायाविमोहितौ तौ अपि (केशवम् उक्तवन्तौ) —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 1.93 (‘fought … for five thousand years’); the second gives the subject of a new sentence whose verb, उक्तवन्तौ, comes in 1.95.
mantras.lit: for five thousands of years, the all-pervading one, with his arms as weapons. And those two, maddened by excessive strength, deluded by Mahāmāyā,
mantras.tr: for five thousand years, the all-pervading Lord fighting with his bare arms. Then the two, drunk with their own great strength and deluded by Mahāmāyā,

comm.t: The battle lasts five thousand years, Viṣṇu fighting with his arms alone, and is not decided by force. It turns when Mahāmāyā clouds the asuras’ minds — the first of Brahmā’s requests (1.86) fulfilled.
The compound महामायाविमोहितौ takes up Medhas’s teaching: Mahāmāyā draws even the minds of the wise into delusion (1.55–56). The asuras are her first example in the stories.
